submission.natural_language_explanation: L10/N2811+ is a discourse-register detector for expository, informational prose about technical subject matter: it is active throughout text of the kind found in scientific abstracts, encyclopedia/reference articles, patents and technical reports, and is essentially silent in dialogue, chat-style Q&A, imperative instructions, promotional copy and personal narrative, even when those use the same scientific vocabulary. Within expository prose its peaks land on the relational function words and light verbs that link technical noun phrases (of, with, at, in, has/have/having, provide, contain, relate, consist, exhibit) and on technical nouns (phosphate, sediment, granite, tissue, cortex, properties, basis, surface, region).

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Technical Report 14-B: Late Holocene Sedimentology of the Weston Basin

Abstract. This report summarises the results of a three-year survey of the sedimentary succession preserved beneath the Weston Basin. The basin lies at the eastern margin of the upland block and contains an estimated 240 metres of Quaternary fill. Our objective was to establish how depositional environments changed through the late Holocene and to relate those changes to regional climatic variability.

Methods. Forty-two cores were recovered with a hydraulic piston sampler. Each core was logged at the field station, and subsamples were taken at intervals of 20 centimetres for grain-size analysis, loss-on-ignition and magnetic susceptibility. Ages were obtained from twelve radiocarbon determinations on plant macrofossils and from tephra correlations with the nearby Langley section.

Results. The basal unit consists of poorly sorted gravel and coarse sand that rests directly on weathered granite. Clast composition is dominated by local quartzite with subordinate schist, and the matrix contains abundant iron oxides that impart a reddish colour to the sediment. Up-section, the gravel grades into a laminated silt-clay unit approximately 70 metres thick. This unit exhibits well-developed horizontal lamination, with occasional ripple cross-bedding that indicates deposition in shallow water subject to intermittent currents. Organic content rises sharply above 120 metres depth, and the sediment at this level has a dark, almost black appearance.

A second coarse interval occurs between 95 and 70 metres below the surface. It comprises several stacked fining-upward cycles, each of which begins with a gravel lag and passes upward into fine sand and silt. The cycles are interpreted as the fill of channels that migrated across the basin floor. Pebble fabrics measured in the lower part of each cycle show a preferred orientation aligned with the inferred palaeoflow direction.

Above 70 metres the succession is dominated by massive clay with scattered dropstones. The clay is largely structureless, although thin horizons rich in organic matter are present at several levels. Dropstones range from granules to boulders and occur throughout the unit. Their presence indicates that ice rafting contributed material to the basin during this interval. The clay also contains rare shells of freshwater gastropods, which provide independent evidence for a lacustrine setting.

Discussion. The record can be divided into three phases. During the first phase, coarse alluvial material accumulated on an irregular basement surface. During the second phase, channel systems reworked the earlier deposits and produced the stacked cycles described above. During the third phase, a lake formed across the basin and fine-grained sedimentation prevailed. The transition between the second and third phases appears abrupt in most cores, although in the western part of the basin a transitional facies of interbedded sand and clay is present.

The dropstone-rich interval has no modern analogue in the region. We attribute it to a period of colder climate during which valley glaciers extended down to the basin margin and calved into the lake. This interpretation is supported by the presence of striated clasts in the coarse fraction and by the geochemical composition of the clay, which points to a local source rather than to long-distance transport by rivers.

Conclusions. The Weston Basin contains a continuous record of environmental change spanning the last twelve thousand years. The lower part of the succession reflects fluvial and alluvial processes, whereas the upper part records the establishment and subsequent infilling of a lake. The dropstone horizons mark brief intervals of glacial influence. Future work should focus on higher-resolution dating of the transitional intervals and on the analysis of additional cores from the western margin.

explanation_scores.explanation: L10/N2811+ is a discourse-register detector for expository, informational prose about technical subject matter: it is active throughout text of the kind found in scientific abstracts, encyclopedia/reference articles, patents and technical reports, and is essentially silent in dialogue, chat-style Q&A, imperative instructions, promotional copy and personal narrative, even when those use the same scientific vocabulary. Within expository prose its peaks land on the relational function words and light verbs that link technical noun phrases (of, with, at, in, has/have/having, provide, contain, relate, consist, exhibit) and on technical nouns (phosphate, sediment, granite, tissue, cortex, properties, basis, surface, region).
